Type.evidence_source: The current work, and that of other scholars working in suicidality, isolation, and gender identities (Cleary, 2012; Johnson et al., 2012; Player et al., 2015; Ramirez & Badger, 2014), calls for greater attention to the subtle and often concealed dimensions of isolation, including what produces it, what it feels like in the everyday, and what prevents it being addressed.

Area.evidence_source: of Irish men by Cleary (2012), participants' steadfast resistance to help-seeking for suicidality amid growing social isolation, hopelessness, and a profound lack of belonging was highlighted as being influenced by their alignment to masculine ideals of being strong and independent. Studies have also consistently indicated that because shame is linked to discussing mental illness and potential for appearing (and therefore being) weak, men commonly turn to self-management practices, which for many will include self-medicating with drugs and alcohol (Campbell, Rondon, Galway, & Leavey, 2013; Cleary, 2012; Ramirez & Badger, 2014). Unfortunately, these practices also tended to increase men's estrangement from family, friends, and professional mental health care, and elicit nonsupportive responses from those whom they remain connected to, thus increasing their social isolation and suicidality (Johnson, Oliffe, Kelly, Galdas, & Ogrodniczuk, 2012; Player et al. 2015; Ramirez & Badger 2014).
